questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a change of regime from a change of incumbents within a regime
questions.stem: The transition table lists several routes by which long-serving rulers in the dataset lost office. Which entry is correctly coded as a route by which a regime itself changes?

options.text: A negotiated transition in which the incumbent signs a pact that rewrites the rules of succession
An armed seizure of the presidency carried out by officers of the national guard
options.misconception: treats a military takeover as an ordinary electoral handover

options.text: A constitutional amendment passed by a two-thirds majority of the national assembly
options.misconception: assumes any constitutional change must be a new regime

options.text: A succession confirmed by the constitutional court after the incumbent died in office
options.misconception: confuses succession with the founding of a new regime

questions.explanation: A regime change replaces the rules governing access to office. A pact and a takeover do that, while an amendment and a succession leave the existing regime in place.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rules of access to office changed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a diagram of consent as the basis of legitimacy
questions.stem: A flow diagram in the chronology sheet runs from grievance to dissent to withdrawal of consent. What does the final box represent in this account of legitimacy?

options.text: The point at which the incumbent's legal authority ends automatically
options.misconception: confuses the loss of consent with the legal end of a mandate

options.text: A situation where the incumbent still governs but no longer has active public support
The formal procedure by which a legislature removes a president by impeachment
options.misconception: reads the diagram as a legal procedure, not consent

options.text: A trigger for constitutional reform that follows a collapse of public trust
options.misconception: assumes erosion of consent forces constitutional change

questions.explanation: The diagram treats legitimacy as a stock of consent that erodes through grievance and dissent. Governance continues after consent falls, but the incumbent's claims become contested.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the reciprocal commitments that make a negotiated agreement a pact

stimulus.body: We sat down in the same room as the men who had ordered our arrests three years earlier. There were no cameras and the terms occupied a single page. They kept the ministries of finance and defence for a fixed period. In exchange we accepted that the elections would be free and that the constitution would be ours as well as theirs.

questions.stem: According to the memorandum, which feature most clearly marks the arrangement as a pact rather than a straightforward victory?

options.text: The incoming government accepted a constitution written by the outgoing side
options.misconception: believes the old constitution binds the new leaders

options.text: The outgoing rulers agreed to step down in exchange for legal immunity for their families
options.misconception: thinks a negotiated exit alone makes an agreement a pact

options.text: Both sides accepted a new constitutional order together, and neither could have installed it alone
The election was observed by a mission from a neighbouring state whose report was published in full
options.misconception: reads foreign observation as the defining feature of a pact

questions.explanation: A pact is a negotiated agreement in which former opponents accept a shared constitutional order and bind themselves to it. Neither immunity clauses nor foreign observers define it.
questions.hint: Ask who is bound by the agreed constitutional order.

options.text: Two regime-changing events, the last dated in November 1996
options.misconception: misses the later seizure that ended the old order

options.text: Three regime-changing events, the last dated in March 1997
options.misconception: treats the municipal election as a change of regime

questions.explanation: Only the new constitution and the later seizure replaced the constitutional order itself. Reshuffles and elections work inside the existing regime, so the count is two.
questions.hint: Ask which entries replaced the rules of access to office.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why negotiated handovers and takeovers are grouped as routes of regime change
questions.stem: A reader asks why the table lists negotiated handovers alongside armed takeovers under the same heading of ways a regime can change. Explain the common feature that justifies grouping them.

answer.exemplar: They qualify as routes of regime change because each replaces the existing set of rules governing who may hold power and how office is transferred. A negotiated handover installs an agreed constitutional order, and a takeover dissolves the old order and installs another, so in both cases the regime itself, rather than only the person in office, is replaced.

questions.explanation: The table groups routes, not transfers of office. What the two share is that the rules of access to office are replaced, which distinguishes regime change from ordinary alternation.
questions.hint: Focus on what is replaced, not on how power moved.

options.misconception: reads a structured grievance as a passing mood

questions.explanation: The speaker still obeys but no longer treats the law as binding because of legitimacy, which is a crisis of belief rather than of compliance.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a statutory clause deters a seizure of power

stimulus.body: Any order for the removal of the President shall require the concurring vote of two thirds of all the members of the National Assembly. No measure of removal shall be entertained while the Assembly is dissolved for more than thirty days.

questions.stem: Based on the statutory extract, which effect on coup attempts is the clause most likely to produce?

options.text: It raises the votes needed to remove the president once a coup has already succeeded
options.misconception: confuses impeachment thresholds with a defence of government

options.text: It discourages would-be claimants, since the assembly they need cannot easily remove a president
It makes a long suspension of the assembly a legal route to avoid removal proceedings
options.misconception: reads a safeguard as a loophole for removing the president

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why consolidation outlasts the parties that founded a democracy
questions.stem: Explain why a democracy can be described as consolidated even though the parties that founded it no longer win elections, and state what would show that the consolidation had failed.

answer.exemplar: Consolidation refers to the durability of the constitutional order rather than the continued success of any one party. A democracy is consolidated when incumbents can be replaced through lawful, regular procedures and the losers accept the outcome, so the alternation of parties is evidence of consolidation rather than evidence against it. Consolidation would have failed if alternations had to be achieved by force, or if the opposition refused to accept legitimate defeat.

questions.explanation: Consolidation concerns the survival of the rules, not the fortunes of the parties that created them. The test is whether incumbents can be replaced lawfully and losers accept defeat.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rules survived a change of incumbents.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of coup-proofing rules as a defence against seizure of power

options.text: Because such rules raise the cost of legal removal, while a seizure does not need the rules' consent

questions.stem: In the chronology table, an entry dated 4 May records a cabinet reshuffle and another dated 9 June records a new constitution promulgated. Why does the table code them differently?

options.text: Because the reshuffle happened in a year without elections and the constitution in an election year
options.misconception: invents an electoral-year rule not shown in the table

options.text: Because the reshuffle concerned a single ministry and the constitution concerned many
options.misconception: reduces the distinction to the number of ministries involved

options.text: Because one is a change of personnel and the other replaces the constitutional order
Because the constitution was signed abroad and the reshuffle was signed at home
options.misconception: relies on the place of signature rather than the content

questions.explanation: The table codes events by whether the constitutional order itself is replaced. A reshuffle changes who holds posts inside the existing order; promulgating a constitution replaces that order.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how protective rules can constrain a president's own supporters
questions.stem: Explain why a government might adopt coup-proofing rules that its own party would find awkward if the incumbent ever lost support within the coalition.

answer.exemplar: Coup-proofing rules make removal through constitutional procedures extraordinarily difficult, and that difficulty operates in both directions. The same supermajority threshold that protects an incumbent from a well-supported removal motion also prevents a legitimate majority from removing a president who has fallen out with his own coalition. A government that expects internal divisions may therefore hesitate, because the insurance it buys against the military also insulates the office against the party on which it depends.

questions.explanation: Protective rules bind future incumbents, not only the present one, so they can lock a president in against his own supporters and block a legitimate internal removal.
questions.hint: Ask who would be constrained by the rule in ten years.

questions.explanation: Separate ministries and budgets split the services institutionally, while the retained joint logistics command preserves one functional link. That supports partial separation, not total fragmentation.

options.misconception: confuses the power to block with the power to carry

options.text: A partner with 101 seats, since only an absolute majority can begin to amend the text
options.misconception: sets the threshold at the bare majority instead of above it

questions.explanation: Amendments normally require a qualified majority, so a partner just above half, such as 51 of 200, is the smallest bloc that can carry them alone. A small partner supplies leverage but not the votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Coalition arithmetic at the point of transition
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a bare majority is a weak basis for a durable transition
questions.stem: Explain why a government that commands a bare majority in a new assembly may still need a negotiated agreement with a smaller party before it can claim a durable transition.

answer.exemplar: A bare majority gives the government the votes to pass ordinary legislation, but it depends every day on the goodwill of a few defecting members, and it cannot amend the constitution or complete the institutional arrangements that make the new order credible. A negotiated agreement with a smaller party converts an arithmetic majority into a constitutional majority, spreads responsibility for the settlement and gives the new rules a wider endorsement than the assembly alone can supply. Without that agreement the government rules, but the transition remains unfinished and reversible by the same arithmetic that created it.

questions.explanation: A bare majority governs but cannot amend or entrench the new order without wider support. Negotiating with a smaller partner converts a numerical advantage into a durable settlement.
questions.hint: Ask what the bare majority cannot do on its own.

questions.explanation: The delay and two thirds threshold make legal removal costly, and assembly membership stays under presidential appointment, so a challenger starts behind. The note contains no sunset clause.

options.misconception: dismisses officeholding as evidence altogether

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish sudden breakdown from gradual erosion and the evidence each leaves
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a regime that breaks down suddenly and one that erodes gradually, and say why the two call for different readings of the evidence.

answer.exemplar: Sudden breakdown produces a visible discontinuity: the constitution is suspended, the legislature is dissolved and a new authority announces itself, so the chronology is marked by a sharp break that can be dated with confidence. Gradual erosion produces no such moment. Reforms are legalised one at a time, officials are rotated, courts are weakened and the electorate is demobilised, and each step is legal on its own. Evidence for erosion therefore has to be assembled from a sequence of separate changes and from what the government can no longer do, rather than read off a single date in the record.

questions.explanation: Breakdown is a dated discontinuity, while erosion is a sequence of individually legal steps. That difference determines whether one event or a pattern of changes is the relevant evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change was dated or gradual.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Coalition arithmetic at the point of transition
questions.learningObjective: Infer the leverage of a small bloc from seat shares
questions.stem: The seat table lists the governing alliance at 52 per cent, the main opposition at 30 per cent and a third party at 18 per cent. Which statement about the arithmetic best follows?

options.text: The governing alliance is guaranteed the presidency because it holds more than half the votes
options.misconception: confuses a seat majority with a guaranteed election outcome

options.text: The opposition can block the alliance because a third of the chamber is enough to stop legislation
options.misconception: overstates the veto power of a minority bloc

options.text: The three blocs together are so balanced that no stable arrangement can be built
options.misconception: ignores that a bloc above half can govern alone

options.text: The third party's bloc is decisive for any question needing more than a simple majority

questions.explanation: A 52 per cent bloc passes ordinary business but falls short of the qualified majorities constitutional change needs, so an 18 per cent partner can decide it. Seat strength is no electoral guarantee.
questions.hint: Compare 52 per cent with the threshold for amendment.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute an average annual rate from a sequence of decree counts
questions.stem: The decree table shows 12 emergency decrees in the first year, 9 in the second, 7 in the third and 5 in the fourth. What is the average number of decrees per year over the four years?
questions.explanation: The four annual counts sum to 33, and 33 divided by 4 is 8.25 decrees a year. Averaging only the last two years, or dividing by the wrong number of years, changes the figure.
questions.hint: Add the four yearly counts, then divide by four.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare a legal removal with a seizure of power
questions.stem: In one case a ruler is removed by a court that declares the elections fraudulent; in another, a military faction takes the palace. Which comparison best captures the difference?

options.text: The first removes a ruler through existing rules, the second replaces the lawful order
Both are regime changes, since in both cases the person holding the presidency is replaced
options.misconception: judges the outcome by personnel rather than by the rules

options.text: The first is a regime change, while the second is a dispute within the armed forces
options.misconception: treats a takeover as an internal military quarrel

options.text: The second is a regime change, while the first is only a legal decision about one election
options.misconception: confuses a legal ruling with the continuing existing order

questions.explanation: A court acting under the constitution uses established rules to remove a ruler; a seizure of the palace replaces the arrangement that made the office lawful. Only the second changes the regime.
questions.hint: Ask which case changed the rules and which only the holder.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret subgroup support figures alongside a national average
questions.stem: A survey finds that while overall support for the government has fallen from 55 to 38 per cent, support among those who attend weekly religious services is 71 per cent. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: The overall figure of 38 per cent must be wrong, because the religious sample shows support of 71
options.misconception: treats a subgroup figure as voiding the national average

options.text: The legitimacy crisis is uneven, since support persists among a specific social group
The government has regained support, because attendance at religious services has increased
options.misconception: assumes rising attendance proves rising approval

options.text: Support has fallen uniformly across all groups, and the religious figure is a recording error
options.misconception: denies the subgroup difference visible in the data

questions.explanation: A national average can fall while a subgroup stays strongly supportive, which is what the two figures show. The crisis is concentrated outside the attending group.
questions.hint: Compare the national average with the subgroup figure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the stabilising and the constraining effects of a pact
questions.stem: Explain why a pact can stabilise a new democratic order and also lock in disadvantages for the parties that agreed to it.

answer.exemplar: A pact works by making the new constitutional order acceptable to the losers as well as the winners. Former rulers who are guaranteed offices, protections or a share of power have reason to respect the settlement, and the opposition that negotiated it has reason to keep it because the terms are written down and enforced by institutions it helped build. The same arrangement also fixes the terms for those who agreed to them. They cannot later reopen the distribution of ministries, the electoral rules or the guarantees to their former opponents without breaking the bargain, so an agreement designed to end conflict can make a particular division of advantage permanent.

questions.explanation: A pact binds the losers to the new order, which stabilises it, and fixes the terms they accepted, which entrenches an unequal division of advantage. Both follow from the same bargain.
questions.hint: Ask what the winners and losers are each unable to undo.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Infer preparation and planning from dated archival entries

stimulus.body: The minutes for 12 April record the president's dissolution of the assembly by decree. A marginal note in the secretary's hand reads: prepared before the vote, held in reserve since January. The following entry, dated 30 April, records elections being announced for August.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the chronology is best supported by the note?

options.text: The dissolution was a reaction to the assembly's vote, since the vote took place earlier that day
options.misconception: invents a same-day vote absent from the entries

options.text: The election announcement in August was forced by pressure from the assembly
options.misconception: attributes the elections to pressure not in the note

options.text: The note indicates that the chronology has been tampered with by the secretary
options.misconception: reads an explanatory marginal note as evidence of forgery

options.text: The dissolution was prepared in advance, and the elections in August were part of the same plan

questions.explanation: The marginal note says the dissolution was prepared in advance and held in reserve, and the next entry records elections for August, pointing to a prearranged sequence.
questions.hint: Read the marginal note as evidence about timing.
